The bill would redefine marriage as a union of two people, removing the current restriction to a man and a woman.
It would recognise same-sex marriages performed overseas and create a new category of religious marriage celebrants who can refuse to solemnise marriages against their beliefs.
Religious bodies would be allowed to refuse facilities, goods or services consistently with their doctrine, matching existing exemptions under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984.
Redefines marriage to a union of two people regardless of sex or gender.
Allows ministers of religion to refuse to solemnise marriages that conflict with their religious doctrine.
Extends the exemption in the Sex Discrimination Act to cover conduct authorised by the Marriage Act.
Ministers of religion, religious marriage celebrants, bodies established for religious purposes, and same-sex couples.

The majority voted in favour of keeping particular parts of [schedule 1](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbills%2Fs1099_first-senate%2F0001%22;rec=0) unchanged. In parliamentary jargon, they voted for "*section 39DD and subsection 39DE(3) in item 8, and items 9 to 16 and 57, of schedule 1 [to] stand as printed.*" This division took place after Liberal Senator [David Fawcett](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/david_fawcett) moved that that parts [be opposed](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-11-28.16.1). These parts deal with the issue of religious marriage celebrants (including how to identify them), who are allowed to discriminate on the basis of their religious beliefs in certain circumstances. ### Why did some Liberals vote Yes and others No? The Liberal Party was split on this issue, with some voting Yes and others voting No. This split within the party is unusual but, given the nature of the subject matter of the vote, the Liberal Party decided to run this as a free vote, meaning that its members could vote however they chose rather than having to vote along party lines. ### What does this bill do? This [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/s1099) will allow same-sex couples to marry under Australian law. However, it will also: > *enable ministers of religion, religious marriage celebrants, chaplains and bodies established for religious purposes to refuse to solemnise or provide facilities, goods and services for marriages on religious grounds; and make amendments ... to provide that a refusal by a minister of religion, religious marriage celebrant or chaplain to solemnise marriage in prescribed circumstances does not constitute unlawful discrimination.* Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd054).

The speaker argued that Parliament should pass the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 in a businesslike manner, noting that 79.5% of Brisbane voters supported same-sex marriage in the postal survey and that the bill strikes a balance between marriage equality and religious protections.

The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, arguing it would end the marginalisation of same-sex couples and expand the freedom to marry while protecting religious freedom and free speech, and noted the 76.3% "yes" vote from his electorate of Goldstein.

The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, passed by the Senate with 43 votes in favour and 12 against, should be passed unamended by the House of Representatives to deliver marriage equality as supported by a majority of Australians. Specific protections for religious celebrants and bodies were read out, and the speaker thanked senators including Penny Wong, Louise Pratt, Dean Smith, and Janet Rice, as well as advocates like Anna Brown, Rodney Croome, and Alex Greenwich.

The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 is an acceptable compromise that will finally allow same-sex marriage, while acknowledging the hurt caused by years of delay and the postal survey, which resulted in a 40% spike in mental health service demand for LGBTI people. They credited Labor figures including Bill Shorten, Louise Pratt, Penny Wong, and others for advancing marriage equality, and noted the bill creates new religious exemptions for civil celebrants.

The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment Bill, arguing that the national survey result obliges parliament to enact marriage equality, while religious freedom concerns should be addressed separately by the expert panel led by Philip Ruddock.

The speaker announced they will vote for the Marriage Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it is a cross-party parliamentary initiative, not a government one, and criticised the Prime Minister's characterisation of the debate as ungracious. They opposed amendments to protect religious freedom, citing a letter from Anglican bishops, and highlighted the postal survey's flaws, noting a 50.1% participation rate in their electorate of Lingiari and low engagement among Aboriginal communities and young people.

The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, arguing it would not affect religious freedom but would strengthen marriage by allowing same-sex couples to marry, and noted that the Australian people led the parliament through the postal ballot.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to allow the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 to be debated in government time, extend the sitting until midnight, defer divisions until 9:30 am on 6 December 2017, and delay any quorum count until the following morning.

The member for Fisher announced his support for the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing the 61.6% national and 62.8% local support in the postal survey, and argued for stronger protections of religious freedoms for the nearly five million Australians who voted no. He also criticised Labor and the Greens for blocking the plebiscite.

The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 without amendments, noting that 62.8% of the Herbert electorate (48,110 people) voted yes in the postal survey, and criticised the $122 million spent on the survey.

The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, favouring marriage equality and opposing amendments that would roll back anti-discrimination protections. The speaker criticised the postal survey as expensive, divisive and hurtful, and noted that while the electorate of Barton returned a 'no' vote, the speaker had consistently supported equality.

The electorate of Farrer voted 55% in favour of same-sex marriage in the postal survey, with a 77.4% participation rate. The speaker supported the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing local advocates including Georgia Henderson, Toni Johnson of Hume Phoenix, Archdeacon Peter Macleod Miller, and Hay Mardi Gras organiser Kerry Aldred, and noted that a review of religious freedom protections led by Philip Ruddock will report in March 2018.

The speaker argued in favour of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, noting that 84% of Corio electors participated in the postal survey and 68% voted yes, and named Magda Szubanski as a key campaign figure. They also called for protecting religious freedoms and quoted Thomas Marshall on the meaning of marriage equality.

The speaker supported the traditional definition of marriage, citing his own 30-year Catholic marriage, while respecting differing views and noting that the same-sex marriage survey returned an emphatic 'yes' in Queensland. He also highlighted that local priorities in his electorate of Groom include the economy, jobs, and infrastructure like the Toowoomba Second Range Crossing.

The speaker tabled the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights’ scrutiny reports 12 and 13 of 2017 and annual reports for 2014–15 and 2015–16, noting that since the 45th Parliament commenced in August 2016 the committee examined 405 bills and 2,942 instruments, with 309 bills and 2,875 instruments assessed as promoting or permissibly limiting human rights or not engaging human rights.

The speaker announced he would vote for same-sex marriage based on the 68% yes vote in his electorate of Moore, despite his personal belief that marriage is for biological parents raising children. He argued the bill needs amendments to protect freedom of speech, religion, parental rights, and faith-based organisations, citing 4,873,987 no voters and examples like legal action against Archbishop Porteous.

The speaker announced they would vote yes on the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, urging no amendments, no excuses and no more delays, and noted a 63.7% yes vote in Western Australia and 71.5% in their electorate of Perth.

The speaker announced they would vote yes on marriage equality and oppose the Prime Minister and member for Warringah's amendments, arguing those amendments would allow businesses like florists and taxis to discriminate against same-sex couples, which they said is wrong and comparable to outlawed racial discrimination.

The speaker argued in support of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, stating that marriage equality is consistent with liberal and conservative values, and that denying same-sex couples the right to marry perpetuates discrimination. The speaker noted 45,000 Australian households with children of same-sex couples would benefit, and affirmed that religious protections in the bill are adequate, opposing unnecessary amendments.

The speaker argued that the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017 should pass, citing the clear 'yes' vote in the postal survey (61.6% nationally, 70% in his electorate of Wills), and opposed any amendments that would weaken existing anti-discrimination laws, while noting the $122 million postal survey was a wasteful abrogation of parliamentary responsibility.

The member for Flynn announced he would vote for the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, citing the 2016 election promise and the 62% national yes vote in the postal survey, with 76% of his electorate supporting the change.

The speaker argued in support of the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Bill 2017, calling it a significant step toward equality for LGBTIQ Australians. The Australian government introduced the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 to modernise media regulation, including repealing broadcasting licence fees and datacasting charges, abolishing the 75% audience reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media control rule, and extending anti-siphoning reforms, with a $4.6 million annual transitional support package for 19 broadcasters. The bill also increases local content obligations for regional television licensees following a trigger event and is part of a broader reform package announced on 6 May 2017, supported unanimously by the media industry.

The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 introduces a new spectrum tax to replace broadcasting licence fees, raising about $40 million annually and providing overall fee relief for broadcasters, with regional broadcasters paying significantly less based on transmitter power and spectrum use. The bill is part of the government's Broadcast and Content Reform Package, has unanimous industry support, and is contingent on the passage of the Broadcasting Reform Bill.

Labor supported the majority of the broadcasting reform bills but opposed repealing the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, warning it would worsen Australia’s already high media ownership concentration and harm diversity, and criticised the government’s piecemeal approach for lacking holistic, evidence-based reform.

The speaker argued for the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, which abolishes the 75 per cent reach rule and the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, introduces higher local content obligations for regional commercial television licensees after ownership changes, and abolishes broadcasting licence fees while maintaining other diversity rules and the anti-siphoning list for major sporting events.

The speaker argued against repealing the two-out-of-three rule, which limits media owners to two of three platforms (radio, TV, newspaper) in a market, citing that Murdoch-owned titles account for 64.2% of metropolitan circulation and Fairfax 26.4%, and that further concentration would harm democratic diversity. They supported other measures in the bill, including licence fee relief, but opposed removing the ownership restriction.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is necessary to modernise Australian media law, citing the 90% decline in Prime Media's value over a decade and a 14% drop in newspaper advertising in 2016, and supported abolishing the two-out-of-three and 75% ownership rules, reducing broadcast licence fees, banning gambling ads during children's sports broadcasts, revising the antisiphoning list, and providing a $30 million package for women's and niche sports on subscription TV.

The government argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 will abolish broadcasting licence fees, introduce a spectrum tax, and remove the 75% audience reach rule and two-out-of-three rule while maintaining protections for local content and competition, with the package having unanimous media industry support.
The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 supports the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017, particularly regarding spectrum fees, and was commended to the House.

Labor will not oppose the two amendments to the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 concerning programming requirements and trigger events, but argued the government’s media reform deal was made behind closed doors, citing 61% voter disapproval, $30 million in taxpayer-funded handouts to Fox Sports, and unanswered questions about a journalism innovation fund.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 is opposed by 61% of Australians and will cause job losses in regional Australia, not job creation. They criticised government deals with crossbenchers, including a $60 million fund for the Nick Xenophon Team and a competitive neutrality inquiry targeting the ABC.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 is urgently needed to help Australian media businesses compete with global internet companies, and criticised the shadow minister for opposing the reforms with illogical arguments, including a claim that industry support for the bill disqualified it.

The speaker argued the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 would deliver up to $4 billion in concessional loans for farm businesses and water infrastructure, noting $680 million already approved to 1,275 farms. Climate change is the greatest challenge facing Australian farmers, with the Garnaut review predicting unchecked climate change would destroy 98% of Murray-Darling Basin farmland, and the government's emissions reduction fund is underfunded and ineffective.

Government amendments to the Regional Investment Corporation Bill 2017 were moved to expand the board from three to between three and five members, with corresponding changes to quorum and vacancy provisions. Crimes Legislation Amendment (Law Enforcement Integrity, Vulnerable Witness Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2013

The Coalition supported the Crimes Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 as making sensible technical changes to investigations and prosecutions of people-smuggling crew, but strongly criticised the rushed 40-hour submission period that undermined public scrutiny and Senate committee processes. Specific provisions included removing wrist X-rays for age determination due to scientific concerns and placing the burden of proof on the prosecution to establish a person was an adult at the time of an offence.
